summary: Describes use cases for peering of non-VoIP services, such as presence and instant messaging, between two or more service providers. The aim is to drive requirements for peering so users in different providers can collaborate with each other. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Two chat companies want their users to message each other, like two phone companies connecting calls. This lists the situations where that would be useful, to help design how it should work.

subtitle: Service provider cooperation in real-time collaboration.

tldr.problem: Users want to communicate with others on different instant messaging and presence services, but providers lack a framework for how to interconnect.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5344 describes use cases showing how presence and instant messaging networks can peer, from simple presence subscriptions to federation hubs and clearing houses.
tldr.outcome: The use cases establish requirements for secure, privacy-respecting peering mechanisms that let multiple service providers work together.

today: RFC 5344 established the foundation for understanding presence and messaging federation. While significant standardization has occurred in SIP-based presence and messaging since 2008, the use cases remain relevant. Modern messaging platforms have largely adopted proprietary federation models outside the IETF standards process, though the security and privacy concerns outlined here remain central to any cross-service messaging system.

sections.title: Presence and Messaging Across Networks
sections.content:
Real-Time Collaboration (RTC) services—presence and instant messaging—have become essential for Internet users. While users within a single organization use one provider's service, users increasingly need to interact with those on other providers' networks, similar to how phone networks interconnect globally. This RFC describes use cases for how service providers can peer their presence and instant messaging services so their users can collaborate across provider boundaries.

The document captures how presence and instant messaging are currently used within enterprises and operator domains, describing practical scenarios that drive requirements for secure peering. It focuses on non-VoIP services (VoIP peering is addressed separately) and does not propose new protocols, but rather documents the situations that any future peering protocol will need to handle.
sections.plainLanguage: Different companies run chat services. This document describes situations where people on one company's service need to talk to people on another company's service, to help those companies figure out how to let that happen.

sections.title: Core Peering Scenarios
sections.content:
Simple Interdomain Subscription is the most basic case: a user (Alice@example.com) on one provider wants to subscribe to the presence of a user (Bob@example.net) on another. Instead of Alice connecting directly to Bob's provider, Alice's provider connects to Bob's provider and forwards the subscription request, then passes back notifications when Bob's status changes. This requires a trust relationship where each provider accepts subscriptions only from its own users or from other trusted providers.

List-Based Subscription extends this: Alice can subscribe to a presence list representing multiple users. These lists may be personal (created and maintained by Alice), public (created by an administrator for groups like a support team), or ad-hoc (temporary lists for conference participants or game players). Cross-provider list subscriptions require providers to resolve and handle lists that span their boundaries.

Pager Mode Instant Messaging allows users to send standalone IM messages across providers. This is simpler than session-based messaging because it does not require a back-and-forth conversation session; each message stands alone.

Session-Based Instant Messaging creates a conversation session using the Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP), allowing multiple exchanges between users on different providers. Sessions are stateful and require more coordination than pager-mode messages.

Beyond presence and basic messaging, the RFC mentions potential services including N-way chat (multi-participant conversations across providers), file transfer (sending files between users on different networks), and document sharing.
sections.plainLanguage: Users might want to: check if a friend on another service is online, send one-off messages, have back-and-forth conversations, talk in group chats, or share files. Each needs different kinds of connections between providers.

sections.title: Authorization and Privacy Across Providers
sections.content:
A critical issue for cross-provider peering is authorization migration. When many users from Provider A watch users in Provider B, a naive approach sends separate presence documents to each user, respecting their privacy rules. However, if Alice and Bob both watch Carol on Provider B, Provider B must send two copies of Carol's presence (filtered for Alice and Bob respectively), creating redundant traffic.

To make this efficient, providers can agree to share privacy information. Provider B sends a single, full copy of Carol's presence document to Provider A, and Provider A becomes responsible for filtering it according to Carol's delegated privacy rules before sending results to its users. This optimization requires both providers to trust each other with sensitive privacy information.

An alternative approach sends multiple copies of the presence document, each tagged with the list of watchers it is intended for, without fully sharing privacy policies. For example, Provider B might send one document showing Carol's location (for users allowed to see it) and another without location information (for users not allowed to see it), each with an associated watcher list.

Privacy protection is essential: users must trust that their presence information is not revealed to unauthorized parties and that sensitive information like block lists remains confidential when passed between providers.
sections.plainLanguage: If many people on one service watch the same person on another, sending them all the person's status separately wastes bandwidth. Providers can agree to share privacy rules, but this requires them to trust each other with sensitive information.

sections.title: Federation Models and Clearing Houses
sections.content:
Federation enables peering between multiple service providers. It can be organized in two ways: peer-to-peer (each provider connects directly to others) or through a central hub called a Clearing House.

A Clearing House is a central service that provides a hub for multiple providers. It offers several functions: authorized interconnection that lets each provider securely verify the identity of other providers; central logging (instead of each provider logging all cross-provider messages, the Clearing House does it centrally); lawful interception services; and support for multi-party services like N-way chat across multiple providers.

Text-based services like presence and messaging consume less bandwidth than VoIP, making them particularly suited to Clearing House models. A central service can efficiently handle logging and other functions that would be expensive if duplicated across many providers. The Clearing House becomes a trusted intermediary in the federation, responsible for accurate forwarding of presence updates and messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Providers can connect directly to each other, or they can all connect to one central hub. The hub can be trusted to log messages, verify which providers are real, and handle complex features like group conversations involving multiple services.

sections.title: Security and Trust Requirements
sections.content:
Peering between providers raises several security requirements. Providers must verify:

  • All communication channels between providers are authenticated and encrypted.
  • Each provider is actually who it claims to be.
  • The other provider is trustworthy and will not leak information to third parties.
  • The other provider will not modify or falsify presence or messaging data except as allowed by authorization policies.
  • Any Clearing House involved is similarly secure.

Users themselves have additional concerns. Presence contains more sensitive information than email addresses; users need assurance their presence is seen only by authorized viewers. Privacy violations could be severe: for example, if a user discovers they are on a friend's block list through information leakage.

The optimization of sharing privacy policies between providers (Section 3) heightens these concerns. The RFC acknowledges these security issues but notes that the document itself does not propose solutions. However, any protocol enabling the peering scenarios described here must address these security requirements comprehensively. Security is not an optional add-on but fundamental to making cross-provider peering acceptable to both administrators and users.
sections.plainLanguage: When messages and presence pass between services, they must be encrypted, service providers must trust each other, and users must be sure their private information stays private. The biggest risk is accidentally revealing who someone is blocked by or other sensitive details.
